notes.text: The former rain — The autumn rain which is needful to mellow the earth and fit it to receive the corn. The latter rain - Needful to bring forward and ripen the fruits, accounted the latter rain because these husbandmen and vine-dressers reckoned from seed time to spring and harvest. The first month - That is, our March.
The fats — The vessels into which the liquor ran out of the press.
Restore — Make up to you.
Wondrously — In one year giving as much as the locusts wasted in the years foregoing. Ashamed - Neither disappointed of your hopes, nor necessitated to seek relief among the heathen.

Afterward — After the return out of Babylon, after the various troubles and salvations by which these may know that I am the Lord. I will pour - In extraordinary gifts on the first preachers of the gospel, and in various graces to all believers. Upon all flesh - Before these gifts were confined to one particular nation; but now they shall be enlarged to all nations, and all that believe. Shall prophesy - This was in part fulfilled according to the letter in the first days of the gospel; but the promise means farther, by pouring out of the spirit on your sons and your daughters, they shall have as full a knowledge of the mysteries of God's law, as prophets before time had. Shalt dream dreams - This also was literally fulfilled in the apostles days. But it may mean farther, the knowledge of God and his will, shall abound among all ranks, sexes and ages in the Messiah's days, and not only equal, but surpass all that formerly was by prophesy, dreams, or visions.
My spirit — Of adoption and sanctification.

Wonders — They who read what historians report of these times, will see this fulfilled in the very letter. Blood - Possibly eruption of blood, as some fountains have been reported to have run with blood, prefiguring the great effusion of blood by the sword, and wars following. Fire - Either breaking out of the earth, or lightning in the air.

The sun — Having mentioned the prodigies which were to be wrought on earth, he now specifies what shall be done in heaven. The terrible day - The unholy day of the destruction of Jerusalem; typifying the day of judgment.

Whosoever shall call — Who hearing the gospel repents and believes in Christ. Delivered - Either from those outward afflictions, or which is infinitely better from eternal miseries, which will swallow up the unbelieving world; "and it will aggravate the ruin of those who perish, that they might have been saved on such easy terms." Is it then easy for a non-elect to repent and believe? May he not as easily pull the sun out of the firmament? In Mount Zion - In the true church typified by Zion. Jerusalem - In mystical Jerusalem, the church and the city of the Messiah. Deliverance - Temporal and eternal. Shall call - To believe in Christ, and by him to wait for eternal life. This chapter has been partly fulfilled in the several deliverances of the Jews, and will have its full accomplishment at the great day. It contains a prophecy of God reckoning with the enemies of his people, ver. 1-8. Of his openly judging all nations, ver. 9-17. And of the provision he has made for his people, ver. 18-21.

Approach — To draw near to God in his house and ordinance, by prayer and praise, and other acts of communion with him. Satisfied - With the blessings there conferred upon thy people, the favour and fellowship of God, remission of sins, renovation of heart and life, joy and peace, and well-grounded assurance of eternal life.

Righteousness — By virtue of thy faithfulness, and goodness. Wilt thou - Thou wilt graciously answer our prayers. The confidence - Thou art the stay and support of all mankind, by thy powerful and gracious providence.
Tumult — No less wild and impetuous.

Thy tokens — Terrible thunders and lightnings, and earthquakes, and comets or other strange meteors, or works of God in the air. Morning - The successive courses of the morning and evening; or of the sun and moon which go forth at those times. Thus the whole verse speaks of the natural works of God, the former clause, of such as are extraordinary and terrible, the latter of such as are ordinary and delightful.

River — With rain, which he very significantly calls a river for its plenty, and the river of God, of God's immediate providing. Them - The inhabitants of the earth. Provided - Or, disposed, the earth, which without this would be hard and barren.
Bringest down — For the rain dissolves the high and hard clods of earth.
Wilderness — Which though neglected by men, are furnished with food for beasts.

Sing — They are abundantly satisfied with thy goodness, and in their manner sing forth the praise of their benefactor. The psalmist calls on all people to praise God, for his sovereign power over the whole creation, ver. 1-7. For his special favour to his people, ver. 8-12. Praises him for his goodness to himself in particular, ver. 13-20. To the chief musician, A song or psalm.

glossa.text: *It becometh thee.* Not the gods of the nations, and not elsewhere, save in contemplation, that is, in faith, and there out of good works *the vow shall be paid,* in the heavenly Jerusalem, the vow which those men used to pay to Mars after battles, and to the other gods in this fashion. *Sion.* Sion is the heavenly country, the same is Jerusalem.

*Hear my prayer.* ((CASS.)) He first does what he says is to be done by the rest, namely, *hear. All flesh.* ((AUG.)) That is, man, that is, out of every kind: poor, rich, men, women, learned, unlearned, boys, old men.

*The words of the wicked.* ((CASS.)) In what hope dost thou pray this? Because *to thee all flesh shall come,* not the soul only, but the evil man also. It is necessary that thou hear. For the words of the wicked are the words of the devil and of our first parents Adam and Eve. *They have prevailed.* That is, they cast us into exile, or the pagans persuaded their own rites to their sons, but thou wilt be merciful in the sacrifice of Christ. ((AUG.)) *The words of the wicked,* that is, we have followed the evil rites and manners of our parents (who, as in age, so in authority, surpass boys). *Thou wilt be merciful.* ((AUG.)) Propitiation is made through the sacrifice which the priest offered, Christ. The priest and the victim are therefore the same.

*Blessed is he whom thou hast chosen,* etc. ((CASS.)) And blessed is every man whom thou hast chosen out of the mass of the lost. *You have not chosen me, but I you ((Joan. XV))*, and thou hast taken him into thy lot, into eternal rest. ((AUG.)) Or thus, thou wilt be merciful through the blessed man: etc., *as far as* things which cannot be told. *In the good things.* ((CASS.)) Which things are good, holiness in oneself, equity toward one's neighbour. *The temple.* The Church, or the flesh of Christ.

*Wonderful.* ((AUG.)) Not in outward things, like a house of earth, but in justice, which is fairer to the inward eye and more lovely, and which we ought now to hunger for, that then we may be filled with it. *In equity.* ((CAS.)) When he shall render to each what is worthy, to whom [each] shall also say: *Hear us, thou who art the Saviour. The hope of all.* He describes the praises of God, and his powers. *And in the sea afar off.* ((AUG.)) Therefore afar off, because in the sea. The sea is spoken of as a figure of the world, bitter with the falsehood of iniquities, and stormy with the tempests of temptations, where the fishes devour one another.

*Preparing the mountains.* ((AUG.)) For fitting uses. *In thy strength.* Because through them he wrought miracles. How did he prepare them? Girded with power, that is, with Deity, because the humanity of the Word is girded about with majesty, so that what the man had not, the Deity might give. *Girded. ((Ibid.))* Christ in the midst, girded on every side, because we all alike have him who believe in him, but because faith is not from us, but from him, he is said to be girded with his own might.

*Who troublest the depth of the sea.* Behold, he who through those prepared ones wrought it, troubling them unto penitence. The depth of the sea, not the surface, but hearts more deeply sunk, or the hearts of princes. These were troubled, when they saw both their gods and their hopes come to nothing. *The noise.* ((AUG.)) Sounding with contradiction, tossing with persecution, etc., *as far as* while they perceive that these prevail more than their own gods.

*The morning and the evening.* ((AUG.)) The morning is prosperity, because the morning is glad after the sadness of the night. The evening is adversity; in these a man is tempted, but it is granted him to go out thence, lest he be caught by gains, he to whom riches are God: lest he be terrified by adversities, he for whom the Lord suffered. *Thou wilt delight.* Thou wilt make them delightful even in this life. For if the going out itself does not delight a man, he does not labour to go out thence, but is caught by gains, he to whom the promise of Christ is not pleasing. And he is terrified by adversities, whom he does not delight who was willing to suffer for him, that he might make a going out for him.

*Thou hast visited the earth and hast inebriated it.* Through preachers wilt thou do this, for within thou teachest those to whom they preach.

*A river.* Of the deep, for the receiving, it is filled with waters, with the gifts of the Holy Ghost, for thou hast prepared food. *The river of God.* ((CAS.)) The mercy of God is compared to a river in full flood, etc., *as far as* as it is disposed by him, without whom nothing is done there.

*Its streams.* The Apostles and others, who drank of the river. *Inebriate them,* that they may suffice for themselves and for others. *Multiply,* that through successions preaching may not fail. *The crown of the year,* the whole world, where the Church is. *Its streams. ((Ibid.)) Thou hast prepared,* etc. And, O Lord, etc., *as far as* whereby the Word of God grows. *The crown of the year. ((Ibid.))* Because the glory of victory belongs to him who conquers the devil. *Of thy bounty,* etc. ((AUG.)) Let no one glory in his own merits.

*Thy fields shall be filled.* ((CASS., AUG.)) Men, because of their evenness, that is, the just. *The hills,* because God raises up the humble *The desert:* all the Gentiles, to whom no prophet was sent.
*The beautiful places of the wilderness shall grow fat.* When the Apostles came to them, through whom they were made comely.

*Valleys. ((Ibid.))* Lowly peoples shall bring forth much fruit. *They shall cry out. ((Ibid.))* *Clamabuut* Not in blasphemy, but in a hymn, thence they abound with corn.

This psalm is sung at the funerals of the faithful, because it treats of the return from the Babylon of this world to the heavenly country, to which the saints, led forth from the flesh at their death, happily pass over, receiving the single robe, until in the resurrection they be glorified with the robe of a twofold beatitude.

notes.text: The time of my departure is at hand — So undoubtedly God had shown him. I am ready to be offered up - Literally, to be poured out, as the wine and oil were on the ancient sacrifices.

The crown of that righteousness — Which God has imputed to me and wrought in me. Will render to all - This increases the joy of Paul, and encourages Timotheus. Many of these St. Paul himself had gained. That have loved his appearing - Which only a real Christian can do. I say a real Christian, to comply with the mode of the times: else they would not understand, although the word Christian necessarily implies whatsoever is holy, as God is holy. Strictly speaking, to join real or sincere to a word of so complete an import, is grievously to debase its noble signification, and is like adding long to eternity or wide to immensity.

glossa.text: *I am poured out as a libation.* We say *libare*: to taste, to pour out, and to immolate. Hence *delibare*, which nevertheless here is put for the immolation itself, for he calls his own passion a *delibatio*. For he is immolated to God who suffers for justice.

*The faith,* which is the head of the Christian religion, *I have kept,* which cannot be had unless God have mercy, because it is the gift of God; whence elsewhere he says: *I have obtained mercy,* not because I was faithful, but *that I might be faithful.* For we find that the Apostle obtained the grace of God with no good merits at all, nay rather with many vices, good things being rendered for evil. He who now, with his passion already drawing near, calls to mind his own good merits, after which he shall obtain the crown; he who after evil merits obtained grace: unless this grace were first freely given, the crown would not be rendered. Therefore his merits are not as though his own, that is, procured for him out of himself, but they are the gifts of God.

*He will render.* For if faith is grace, and eternal life is as it were the wage of faith; God does indeed seem to render eternal life as a debt to the faithful man to whom he owes it, because he has merited it through faith; but because faith is grace, and eternal life is grace, therefore he will render it through grace. *A just judge.* Assuredly just in repaying good things for good, because nevertheless he is first merciful in repaying good things for evil; the very justice by which good things are repaid for good is not without mercy.

notes.text: He spake this parable — Not to hypocrites; the Pharisee here mentioned was no hypocrite, no more than an outward adulterer: but he sincerely trusted in himself that he was righteous, and accordingly told God so, in the prayer which none but God heard.

I fast twice in the week — So did all the strict Pharisees: every Monday and Thursday. I give tithes of all that I possess - Many of them gave one full tenth of their income in tithes, and another tenth in alms, the sum of this plea is, I do no harm: I use all the means of grace: I do all the good I can.
The publican standing afar off — From the holy of holies, would not so much as lift up his eyes to heaven - Touched with shame, which is more ingenuous than fear.
This man went down — From the hill on which the temple stood, justified rather than the other - That is, and not the other.

glossa.text: *Two men.* Because the parable by which he invited to prayer he so concluded as to say that, when the Judge comes, faith would hardly be found on earth. Lest anyone should flatter himself with a superfluous knowledge of faith, or even with a confession of it, in this parable he shows more diligently that not the words of faith but the works are to be examined by God, among which humility chiefly reigns; and because the proud do not have it, presuming upon their own righteousness and despising the weak, they, as though empty of faith, are not heard when they pray.

*God, I give thee thanks,* etc. There are four kinds of swelling: when either a man reckons that the good which he has he has of himself; or, if he believes it given by God, he thinks it given for his merits; or when he boasts that he has what he has not; or when, despising the rest, he seeks to be seen singularly to have what he has. With this plague the Pharisee laboured, who therefore went down not justified, because ascribing to himself singularly the merits of good works, he set himself before the publican.

*I fast twice.* Behold, the Pharisee has an eye to the showing of abstinence, to the obtaining of mercy, to the returning of thanks to God; to the keeping of humility he has none. And what does it profit if the whole city be guarded, and one opening be left through which the enemies may enter?

*And the publican.* As a humble man, he does not dare to draw near, that God may draw near to him: he does not look up, that he may be looked upon; he presses down his conscience, but lifts up his hope; he strikes his breast, he exacts penalties of himself that God may spare; he confesses that God may pardon; God pardons what he acknowledges. *God, be merciful.* The publican praying humbly belongs to those of whom it is said: Shall not God revenge his elect crying to him? The Pharisee boasting of his merits belongs to those of whom it is added: *The Son of man coming, thinkest thou, shall he find faith on earth?*
*For every one,* etc. The controversy of the Pharisee and the publican being set down, the sentence of the judge is set down, that pride may be shunned.

echoes.text: In this way you shall offer daily, for seven days, the food of the offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh. It shall be offered in addition to the continual burnt offering, and its drink offering.
echoes.note: Paul says 'I am already being offered' (poured out as a drink offering), drawing on the sacrificial libation prescribed in the Mosaic cult. The image of life poured out like the wine offering at the altar gives his coming death a cultic, sacrificial coloring.

echoes.text: Therefore will they receive the crown of royal dignity And the diadem of beauty from the Lord’s hand; Because with his right hand will he cover them, And with his arm will he shield them.
echoes.note: The 'crown of righteousness' which the righteous Judge will award echoes Wisdom's promise that the righteous 'shall receive a glorious kingdom and a beautiful crown from the Lord's hand.' The eschatological reward of a crown from God's hand to the righteous is shared imagery.

echoes.text: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.
echoes.note: The title 'the righteous judge' who will give the crown 'on that day' reuses the enthronement-psalm refrain that the LORD comes to judge the world in righteousness. The forensic epithet is colored by the Old Testament confession of God as righteous judge of all.

echoes.text: Yes, take silver and gold, and make crowns, and set them on the head of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest; and speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple; even he shall build Yahweh’s temple; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule on his throne; and he shall be a priest on his throne; and the counsel of peace […]
echoes.note: The laying-up of a crown for the faithful may faintly recall the crowns set in the temple of the LORD as a memorial in Zechariah. The notion of a crown stored and later bestowed offers a remote Old Testament background to the crown reserved for Paul.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me. Against you, and you only, have I sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight; that you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge. Behold, I was born in iniquity. In sin […]
echoes.note: The tax collector's 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner' closely tracks the penitent's plea in Psalm 51, 'Have mercy on me, O God... blot out my transgressions,' the paradigmatic prayer of the contrite sinner. The shared vocabulary of mercy plus self-identification as sinner and the broken-and-contrite heart God accepts make this a strong verbal-thematic echo. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
echoes.note: The maxim 'God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble' underwrites the closing logion that the self-exalting are humbled and the self-humbling exalted. The Pharisee's proud self-display versus the tax collector's lowliness is precisely this proverb's contrast, and the LXX wording was a standard Second-Temple proof text. Strong coherence with Luke's reversal theme.
echoes.lxxText: The Lord resists the proud; but he gives grace to the humble.

echoes.text: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.
echoes.note: Job 22:29 states that when one is brought low he says 'lift up,' for God saves the lowly of eyes, matching both the exaltation-of-the-humble logion and the detail that the tax collector would not lift up his eyes. The eyes-lowered humility detail strengthens the link beyond the common reversal topos. Medium volume.

echoes.text: thus says the Lord Yahweh: Remove the turban, and take off the crown; this will not be as it was; exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's oracle 'exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high' supplies a prophetic form of the humbled/exalted reversal that concludes the parable. The phrasing is a recognized OT antecedent for Luke's reversal sayings (cf. also 1:52). Thematic rather than verbal-specific here.

echoes.text: ‘Why have we fasted,’ say they, ‘and you don’t see? Why have we afflicted our soul, and you take no knowledge?’ “Behold, in the day of your fast you find pleasure, and exact all your labors. Behold, you fast for strife and contention, and to strike with the fist of wickedness: you don’t fast this day so as to make your voice to be heard on high. Is such the fast that I have chosen? the day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow down his head as a […]
echoes.note: Isaiah 58 rebukes those who fast yet oppress, contrasting empty self-righteous fasting with the fast God chooses (justice and mercy to the poor). The Pharisee's boast of fasting twice a week and tithing, set against the justified penitent, draws on this prophetic critique of cultic display divorced from righteousness. Coherent with Luke's piety-critique.

echoes.text: For thus says the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.
echoes.note: God dwells 'with him who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the heart of the contrite,' which matches why the humbled tax collector goes home justified rather than the proud Pharisee. The contrite/humble spirit that God favors is the theological engine of the parable. Medium coherence.

echoes.text: He that keeps the law multiplies offerings; He that takes heed to the commandments sacrifices a peace offering. He that requites a good turn offers fine flour; And he that gives alms sacrifices a thank offering. To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; And to depart from unrighteousness is an atoning sacrifice.
echoes.note: Sirach insists that keeping the law and almsgiving outweigh mere sacrifice, a Second-Temple critique of confidence in cultic performance like the Pharisee's. Faint and contested, but coherent with the tithing/fasting boast being insufficient. Low volume.

echoes.text: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.
echoes.note: The one who may ascend the temple hill is the clean of hands and pure of heart; the two men 'went up into the temple to pray' and only the contrite one is accepted. The temple-ascent and acceptability motif faintly underlies the scene. Low confidence.

glossa.text: *Sevenfold as much.* A perfect reward, namely. For the number seven, etc., *as far as* but it affords also the working of the four principal virtues.

*Offer not gifts,* etc. With God there is no quantity of the gift; nor is the person of the powerful regarded: but the love and the humility of the heart. Therefore a sacrifice ought not to be offered out of iniquity, but out of just labour.

notes.text: They-That constantly abide in thy house; the priests and Levites, or other devout Jews who were there perpetually, as Anna, Luke ii, 36-37. They will — They are continually employed in that blessed work.
Whose strength — Who trusteth in thee as his only strength. Thy ways - Blessed are they whose hearts are set upon Zion and their journey is thither.

Baca — A dry valley in the way to Jerusalem, here put for all places of like nature. Make a well - They dig divers little pits or wells in it for their relief. The rain - God recompenses their diligence with his blessing, sending rain wherewith they may be filled.
They go — They grow stronger and stronger. Appeareth - This is added as the blessed fruit of their long and tedious journey.

glossa.text: *How lovely.* Behold how great the warfare. *For the sparrow,* how secure.

*For the sparrow,* etc. ((AUG.)) To two he renders two: *the heart* as *the sparrow; the flesh* as *the turtle,* to which he gives also *young ones:* with the heart we think upon God, as the sparrow flies to the house; with the flesh we do works. ((CASS.)) As the sparrow forsakes the woods, and rejoices when a house is found, where it fears no snares: so the soul rejoices, while it knows that a house is prepared for it in heaven. The spirit, which is as a sparrow flying on high, reaching towards God himself. *A nest, etc.* ((AUG.)) *A nest* for a time, *a house* true unto eternity. By the nest therefore he means faith, and the conformity of the sacraments of the Church, which nest the turtle seeks, that she may lay up her young. For she does not cast them anywhere, but in the nest of the Church she does good works wholesomely, for which she is saved: wherein she differs from others who do works, but not in the nest of faith. For the pagans also do works, they clothe the naked, etc., and heretics do many things: but not in the nest of the Church, and therefore they are trodden down, they are not preserved. This flesh is the woman, by whom the sparrow is seduced, but she shall be saved by the bearing of works, if in the nest, that is, if she shall have persevered in faith. But God supplies that whereof the nest may be made, for he clothed himself with the hay of the flesh that he might come to thee. *Thy altars, O Lord.* ((CASS.)) Where souls feast at the heavenly banquet, where the soul may rejoice as in a house. ((AUG.)) And the flesh lays up its works, whence: Blessed are they who, etc., where he shows to what beatitude the warfare leads.

*Blessed are they that dwell in thy house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise thee.* ((AUG.)) This the good have already, namely, that they dwell in thy house. There follows: *For ever and ever they shall praise thee.* This is the whole business of the saints there: there is no necessity there, which is the mother of all human actions, for whom do they do anything there, where none are in need; they have therefore and they act, whence they are blessed. But every blessed one is called blessed by having or by acting.
*Blessed is the man whose help is from thee: he hath disposed ascensions in his heart.* ((CASS.)) By what help one may come to the house.

*In the vale of tears.* ((CASS.)) The vale of tears is the humility of one repenting. ((AUG.)) But whence the weeping: because he afflicted us with the law, through which we knew that sin fights against the spirit, and we groan, namely how we may come to the place which he has appointed, by his power and help assuredly. *In the place which he hath appointed. For he shall give a blessing.* Which cannot be set forth, which eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, that is, the kingdom to come, which God has disposed and ordained, that it may be come to by degrees.

glossa.text: *Two men.* Because the parable by which he invited to prayer he so concluded as to say that, when the Judge comes, faith would hardly be found on earth. Lest anyone should flatter himself with a superfluous knowledge of faith, or even with a confession of it, in this parable he shows more diligently that not the words of faith but the works are to be examined by God, among which humility chiefly reigns; and because the proud do not have it, presuming upon their own righteousness and despising the weak, they, as though empty of faith, are not heard when they pray.

*God, I give thee thanks,* etc. There are four kinds of swelling: when either a man reckons that the good which he has he has of himself; or, if he believes it given by God, he thinks it given for his merits; or when he boasts that he has what he has not; or when, despising the rest, he seeks to be seen singularly to have what he has. With this plague the Pharisee laboured, who therefore went down not justified, because ascribing to himself singularly the merits of good works, he set himself before the publican.

*I fast twice.* Behold, the Pharisee has an eye to the showing of abstinence, to the obtaining of mercy, to the returning of thanks to God; to the keeping of humility he has none. And what does it profit if the whole city be guarded, and one opening be left through which the enemies may enter?

*And the publican.* As a humble man, he does not dare to draw near, that God may draw near to him: he does not look up, that he may be looked upon; he presses down his conscience, but lifts up his hope; he strikes his breast, he exacts penalties of himself that God may spare; he confesses that God may pardon; God pardons what he acknowledges. *God, be merciful.* The publican praying humbly belongs to those of whom it is said: Shall not God revenge his elect crying to him? The Pharisee boasting of his merits belongs to those of whom it is added: *The Son of man coming, thinkest thou, shall he find faith on earth?*
*For every one,* etc. The controversy of the Pharisee and the publican being set down, the sentence of the judge is set down, that pride may be shunned.

echoes.text: In this way you shall offer daily, for seven days, the food of the offering made by fire, of a pleasant aroma to Yahweh. It shall be offered in addition to the continual burnt offering, and its drink offering.
echoes.note: Paul says 'I am already being offered' (poured out as a drink offering), drawing on the sacrificial libation prescribed in the Mosaic cult. The image of life poured out like the wine offering at the altar gives his coming death a cultic, sacrificial coloring.

echoes.text: Therefore will they receive the crown of royal dignity And the diadem of beauty from the Lord’s hand; Because with his right hand will he cover them, And with his arm will he shield them.
echoes.note: The 'crown of righteousness' which the righteous Judge will award echoes Wisdom's promise that the righteous 'shall receive a glorious kingdom and a beautiful crown from the Lord's hand.' The eschatological reward of a crown from God's hand to the righteous is shared imagery.

echoes.text: before Yahweh; for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, the peoples with his truth.
echoes.note: The title 'the righteous judge' who will give the crown 'on that day' reuses the enthronement-psalm refrain that the LORD comes to judge the world in righteousness. The forensic epithet is colored by the Old Testament confession of God as righteous judge of all.

echoes.text: Yes, take silver and gold, and make crowns, and set them on the head of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest; and speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies, “Behold, the man whose name is the Branch: and he shall grow up out of his place; and he shall build Yahweh’s temple; even he shall build Yahweh’s temple; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule on his throne; and he shall be a priest on his throne; and the counsel of peace […]
echoes.note: The laying-up of a crown for the faithful may faintly recall the crowns set in the temple of the LORD as a memorial in Zechariah. The notion of a crown stored and later bestowed offers a remote Old Testament background to the crown reserved for Paul.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me. Against you, and you only, have I sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight; that you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge. Behold, I was born in iniquity. In sin […]
echoes.note: The tax collector's 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner' closely tracks the penitent's plea in Psalm 51, 'Have mercy on me, O God... blot out my transgressions,' the paradigmatic prayer of the contrite sinner. The shared vocabulary of mercy plus self-identification as sinner and the broken-and-contrite heart God accepts make this a strong verbal-thematic echo. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
echoes.note: The maxim 'God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble' underwrites the closing logion that the self-exalting are humbled and the self-humbling exalted. The Pharisee's proud self-display versus the tax collector's lowliness is precisely this proverb's contrast, and the LXX wording was a standard Second-Temple proof text. Strong coherence with Luke's reversal theme.
echoes.lxxText: The Lord resists the proud; but he gives grace to the humble.

echoes.text: When they cast down, you shall say, ‘be lifted up.’ He will save the humble person.
echoes.note: Job 22:29 states that when one is brought low he says 'lift up,' for God saves the lowly of eyes, matching both the exaltation-of-the-humble logion and the detail that the tax collector would not lift up his eyes. The eyes-lowered humility detail strengthens the link beyond the common reversal topos. Medium volume.

echoes.text: thus says the Lord Yahweh: Remove the turban, and take off the crown; this will not be as it was; exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's oracle 'exalt that which is low, and abase that which is high' supplies a prophetic form of the humbled/exalted reversal that concludes the parable. The phrasing is a recognized OT antecedent for Luke's reversal sayings (cf. also 1:52). Thematic rather than verbal-specific here.

echoes.text: ‘Why have we fasted,’ say they, ‘and you don’t see? Why have we afflicted our soul, and you take no knowledge?’ “Behold, in the day of your fast you find pleasure, and exact all your labors. Behold, you fast for strife and contention, and to strike with the fist of wickedness: you don’t fast this day so as to make your voice to be heard on high. Is such the fast that I have chosen? the day for a man to afflict his soul? Is it to bow down his head as a […]
echoes.note: Isaiah 58 rebukes those who fast yet oppress, contrasting empty self-righteous fasting with the fast God chooses (justice and mercy to the poor). The Pharisee's boast of fasting twice a week and tithing, set against the justified penitent, draws on this prophetic critique of cultic display divorced from righteousness. Coherent with Luke's piety-critique.

echoes.text: For thus says the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: “I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite.
echoes.note: God dwells 'with him who is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the heart of the contrite,' which matches why the humbled tax collector goes home justified rather than the proud Pharisee. The contrite/humble spirit that God favors is the theological engine of the parable. Medium coherence.

echoes.text: He that keeps the law multiplies offerings; He that takes heed to the commandments sacrifices a peace offering. He that requites a good turn offers fine flour; And he that gives alms sacrifices a thank offering. To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; And to depart from unrighteousness is an atoning sacrifice.
echoes.note: Sirach insists that keeping the law and almsgiving outweigh mere sacrifice, a Second-Temple critique of confidence in cultic performance like the Pharisee's. Faint and contested, but coherent with the tithing/fasting boast being insufficient. Low volume.

echoes.text: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.
echoes.note: The one who may ascend the temple hill is the clean of hands and pure of heart; the two men 'went up into the temple to pray' and only the contrite one is accepted. The temple-ascent and acceptability motif faintly underlies the scene. Low confidence.

registers.label: Spare
lines: How lovely is your dwelling place, O Lord of hosts.
God, be merciful to us.
The tax collector would not lift his eyes, but beat his breast.
God, be merciful to us.
The Lord hears the cry of the lowly.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Two people go up to pray; one lists his merits, the other can barely raise his head.
God, be merciful to me, a sinner.
And it is the second one — empty-handed, honest, broken open — who goes home justified.
God, be merciful to me, a sinner.
The God of hosts does not despise a contrite heart; he hears the cry of the lowly.
God, be merciful to me, a sinner.
So we come with no merits to count, only mercy to ask, and that is enough.
God, be merciful to me, a sinner!
